The main feature of tox is end-to-end encryption so only you and the person you are sending a message to can see your message. Tox is also decentralized. Most chat apps don't have built in encryption so the company that is running the servers for them (like google) would be able to read all of your messages.

I think the selling point for Tox isn't it's ease of use but its e2e encrypted distributed peer to peer nature. It's goal is to be unmonitorable.

Anyway, I think the previous comments don't quite get what's the point behind Tox. Tox, in terms of Instant Messaging, provides a free, distributed, secure and privacy-protecting communication tool. It does so by in simple terms distributing the whole network among the clients, making each client a potential candidate to act as node and thus route messages of other people. No other common IM tool does this, especially not Skype nor Hangsout nor iWhatever. In those terms, I must say, I am a bit disappointed in the previous comments. We're fucking programmers. If you just eat whatever everyone throws at us without thinking, I don't quite think you're in the right workplace.

What I do know about Tox is that it's quite interesting in that it is also a platform. In theory, every application could use Tox as transport layer (Much like what HTTP is for many web APIs). Think of the possibilities. Please. Just for a moment, ok? Remember Hamachi? That tool giving you a fake LAN so you can play games with friends without having to open ports and shit? Tox could do that. Remember NAT issues with IPv6 DualStack-Lite implementations? Tox can solve that.

I think that it's an already fascinating piece of software. Does it look fabulous? I don't know. I think the Windows Skype client looks like horrific, and I do much prefer the linux Skype client as it gets shit done. As long it works good and I don't have to outright puke from looking at a Tox client (There are many clients btw), I'm fine.
